title: Carpet area disputes - how the law changed the calculation method
p1:
Buying a flat advertised as 1,000 sq. ft.? You might be paying for space you cannot actually use.

For years, homebuyers struggled with confusing area calculations. Builders used different methods to describe flat sizes, making it difficult to know exactly what buyers were getting.
p2:
The biggest change came with the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA).

Under RERA, carpet area has a specific legal meaning. It refers to the net usable floor area inside an apartment, excluding external walls, service shafts, exclusive balconies and verandahs, but including internal partition walls.

Here's the surprising part: internal partition walls are included in carpet area, even though buyers often assume only the open, usable floor space counts.
p3:
This changed the way developers must disclose apartment sizes in RERA-regulated projects.

Builders can no longer freely rely on confusing terms such as super built-up area when making the legally required carpet-area disclosures.

Practical takeaway: Before booking a flat, compare the carpet area mentioned in the agreement with the RERA project details. Don't judge a property only by its advertised square footage or price per square foot.

A smaller advertised number may actually give you a clearer picture of what you are buying.
conclusion: Have you ever discovered that the actual usable space in a flat was much smaller than the area advertised by the builder? Do you think RERA has made carpet-area calculations more transparent for homebuyers?
